cues.text: Hi, Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: It's harder than I expected, but I've got some great classes. How about you?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Not brilliant. I'm really struggling with my Year 12 science class.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Are they hard to control?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Well, I don't have discipline problems as such.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: It's just that they don't seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It's depressing.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: They listen to what I say and I gave them a test last week and the results weren't too bad, but there's no real engagement.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: I was wondering about something on the children's diets, you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Let's think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: OK. But you'd also need to have access to the children's medical records and I don't think people would be happy about that. Confidentiality would be an issue.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant but I suspect it's not going to be easy.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Wouldn't that be upsetting for the children?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Well, the animals don't have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they're given a certain diet and the effects are observed.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Yes. You'd have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it's quite straightforward.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn't necessarily be true for people, would it?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: No, that's true. But the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It's inevitable.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: I suppose so. So, what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Yes, you'd need experimental mice, ones that have been specially bred for experiments.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Well, something to do with nutrition. So, maybe we could look at food supplements, things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Mmm, that might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar that they don't really need?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Exactly. Do they eat it, or do they decide to leave it?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment, adding another variable.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don't do much.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Or I could repeat the experiment, but change the type of food I provided, or use mice with a different genetic structure.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: But I think your idea would be more interesting. I might think about that some more.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Sure, I did a similar experiment in college actually.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Great. So how many mice would I need?
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: I'd say about 12 and all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Okay, and I'd need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: And how would I tell them apart? I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group or just mark them in some way.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: You could use food colouring, that wouldn't hurt them.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Perfect. Then each group would go into a separate cage and one group, let's call them group A, would be the control group.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: So they just have ordinary mouse food. I suppose you can buy that.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they'd also have the extra sugar.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Would you just give them straight sugar?
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: It might be better to give them something like cereal with it.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Hmm. Then you'd need to weigh the mice, I should think, once a week. And you'd need an electronic balance.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: But we can't hold them on the balance, or it'd affect the reading.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Exactly. So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: OK. So once we've measured the weight gain of each mouse, we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation, and then see where we go from there.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: That sounds cool. I think the students will enjoy it.
cues.speaker: Claire

cues.text: Yes. One thing you must remember...
cues.speaker: Jake
